name: Fatima Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work evenings at a big 24-hour superstore out on the ring road, usually two till ten. I start on the tills, then about seven I swap to the self-checkout bank, where I'm basically a referee for eight machines and a lot of grumpy people buying wine. I like the regulars, like the old man who buys one lemon and a newspaper every night just to have a chat. What wears me out is the standing and the beeping, honestly.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how does the money look for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Nine years this spring, since I was eighteen. The pay's decent for a till job because of the evening rate and our union deal, and I've got close to a year of wages saved because I don't spend much. My partner Tomas drives buses for the city, and we're saving for a flat together. I'm a union member and I go to the branch meetings when my shifts let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so, now let's talk about staffing levels instead of robots. In the union group chat I'd be the one posting that the hype was a cover for cutting hours. At work I'd just shrug, because we've heard big promises about new tills before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job stays my job. The self-checkouts already came in four years ago and took six till spots on my shift, so that's the change I already live with. If AI fizzles, the pressure is still there, but it's the same pressure as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my shifts and keep putting four hundred a month into the flat fund. I'd push at branch meetings for a rule that self-checkouts always have two staff, not one. Maybe I'd look at the shift supervisor course next year, but no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relieved, a bit flat. It's like a storm forecast that never comes, so you just get on with the washing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the self-checkouts took six spots. Who did that hit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It hit the older women on days, mostly, people like Brenda who'd been there twenty years. They didn't get sacked, they got their hours cut until they left on their own. That's how it happens in shops, quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So what would the flat fund look like in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd keep going as planned, about two more years and we can put down a deposit. Tomas has a steady council contract, so nothing in this picture changes that. The flat is the one big thing we're both focused on.

say: I'd say the **hype** was mostly a cover for cutting staff hours.
I'd push the union to talk about **staffing levels**, not shiny new tills.
think: My **job stays mine**, because the big change, self-checkouts, already happened four years ago.
The **pressure on hours** stays the same as now, which I already know how to live with.
do: Keep my evening shifts and put **£400 a month** into the flat fund.
Push at branch meetings for **two staff** on every self-checkout bank.
feel: **Relieved** and a little flat, like a storm forecast that never arrives.
S0.quote: The self-checkouts already came in four years ago and took six till spots on my shift, so that's the change I already live with.
fieldNote: She measures AI against **self-checkouts**, the change that already cost her shift six till spots.
Her **union** membership shapes how she reads every new tool: as a staffing question first.
Strong savings and a partner on a **council contract** make the plain future feel genuinely secure.

steps.text: Keep the two-till-ten evening shifts at the superstore
Put 400 a month into the shared flat deposit fund
Push the union branch for two staff on every self-checkout bank

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office jobs getting it first this time, and they should have listened when it happened to us. Online I'd share stuff about a shorter week and making the companies pay in. At work I'd tell the younger ones to join the union now, before anything lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the thinking part is small. The ordering and the rotas are done at head office anyway, so if a computer does them instead I barely notice. The worry is the slow robots, like the shelf-scanning one they trialled last year. Once the shelf-scanning robot works, the night fill crew goes, and then they come for the evening tills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put but start the supervisor course so I'm the one running the machines, not replaced by them. I'd keep saving for the flat, maybe push it to five hundred a month. I'd also volunteer to help the branch write up what staffing rules we want before the robots arrive properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit unsettled, I'd say. I'm fine, but I'd be watching the shop floor differently, counting heads on each shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd use AI now and then. Would that change here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit. I already used one of those chat tools to tidy up a letter to our landlord, and it was good. I'd use it to help write the union stuff, but I'm not going to become a tech person overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kai on nights, who stacks shelves and is brilliant at it but hates screens. If the scanning robots work, his whole crew shrinks first. I'd be worried he'd be the type to just go quiet and leave.

say: I'd say **office jobs** are getting it first, like shop workers did before.
I'd tell younger colleagues to **join the union** before the robots properly land.
think: The **thinking tasks** in my job, like rotas and ordering, already sit at head office.
The real threat is the **shelf-scanning robot**, which would cut night crews first, then evening tills.
do: Start the **supervisor course** so I run the machines rather than get replaced.
Raise flat savings to **£500 a month** and help the branch draft staffing rules.
feel: **Unsettled** but not scared, watching how many heads are on each shift.
S1.quote: Once the shelf-scanning robot works, the night fill crew goes, and then they come for the evening tills.
fieldNote: She sees her work as **hands-on**, so desk-focused change feels distant but robots feel near.
Worry for colleague **Kai** on nights shows how she thinks about the weakest first.
Her plan is a **ladder move** within the store rather than leaving retail.

steps.text: Sign up for the store's shift supervisor course next spring
Raise the flat deposit savings to 500 a month
Help the union branch write staffing rules for robots
Use a chat tool to draft union letters and notes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in now, with a robot tax and income support. I'd be loud about it, marches, petitions, all of it. At work I'd be telling people this isn't a reason to panic but it is a reason to organise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my till job is done by 2031, maybe sooner for the self-checkout side. The ordering and scheduling would go straight away in 2028, but that's not really me. What's me is the scanning, the bagging, the shelf fixing, and once robots can do that, there's nothing left in that store for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd stop dreaming about the supervisor course, because supervising robots isn't going to need many people. I'd look at care work or the buses with Tomas, jobs where you deal with people's bodies and moods. I'd hold the savings tight and maybe put the flat on hold for a year to see how prices go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly, under the angry bit. It's five years from my perfectly normal job to nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we're not buying anything until we know which of us still has a job in 2031. Buses would get driverless too, he knows that. We'd probably sit with a spreadsheet and work out how long one wage and the savings lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work. Why that, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people want a person when they're old and frightened, not a machine. My nan was in a home last year and the carers who held her hand mattered more than anything. I think that lasts longer than a till.

say: I'd demand a **robot tax** and income support from the government straight away.
I'd tell colleagues this is a reason to **organise**, not to panic.
think: My **till job** is likely gone by 2031, once robots can scan, bag and fix shelves.
The **ordering and scheduling** go in 2028, but that work was never really mine.
do: Drop the **supervisor plan** and look into care work or bus driving.
Hold the **savings** tight and pause the flat purchase for about a year.
feel: **Scared** underneath the anger, at five years from a normal job to nothing.
S2.quote: People want a person when they're old and frightened, not a machine.
fieldNote: She separates the **thinking work** that goes in 2028 from her hands-on work that goes later.
The three-year robot gap gives her time to pivot to **care work**, which she trusts.
Strong savings keep her from alarm, but the **flat** is the first thing put on hold.

steps.text: Apply for care assistant jobs at local care homes
Pause buying the flat with Tomas for about a year
Sign and share petitions for a robot tax
March with the union branch for income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, but with more planning: we've got time to set up proper retraining, so let's do it now. I'd push the union to get the company to pay for courses. I'd post about it, but less shouty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I've got until about 2034 on the tills, which is seven years. That's long enough to switch properly instead of grabbing whatever's going. The office side of retail goes in 2031, and I'd watch that as the warning sign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a care qualification part-time next year, evenings off from the shop. I'd keep working the tills until the course is done, then switch. We'd still buy the flat, maybe a cheaper one, because two years from now we'd know more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but steady. It's like having a date for a big exam, which is better than a surprise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut to fit a course in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the Saturday overtime, which is about a hundred and twenty a month. I'd miss the money, but the savings cover it. The course matters more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still push the union, or just look after yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I think. I'd do my course for me, but I'd keep pushing for company-paid retraining for everyone. Think of Brenda and that lot. When the self-checkouts came in, the older day staff got nothing, no course and no help, and I don't want that again for anyone.

say: I'd say there's time to set up **proper retraining**, so we should start now.
I'd push the union to make the company **pay for courses**.
think: I've got until about **2034** on the tills, roughly seven more years.
When office retail jobs go in **2031**, that's my warning sign to move.
do: Start a **care qualification** part-time next year, around shop shifts.
Drop the **Saturday overtime** and buy a cheaper flat a bit later.
feel: **Nervous** but steady, like having a set date for a big exam.
S3.quote: When the self-checkouts came in, the older day staff got nothing, no course and no help, and I don't want that again for anyone.
fieldNote: Five years of warning turns her **panic** into a timetable.
She plans a **care qualification** while still drawing a till wage.
Her memory of colleague **Brenda** drives her push for company-paid retraining.

steps.text: Start a part-time care qualification on weekday evenings
Drop Saturday overtime to make room for study
Push the union for company-paid courses for all staff
Look at cheaper flats for a purchase in two years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this fairly, so no excuses for anyone. I'd talk about it like climate change: we know it's coming, plan for it. At work I'd say it more calmly, because ten years feels far off to most people there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully I'd be thirty-seven when the robots arrive, which is a good age to have already switched. I'd buy the flat, get settled, and change jobs in my early thirties. The tills are fine for a few more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the flat with Tomas next year as planned. I'd do the supervisor course first, then the care course around thirty. I'd keep going to branch meetings to get retraining written into the next deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm, really. Ten years is a lot of life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this one that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That people at work will waste the ten years. Half my shift think it's science fiction. I'd worry they wake up in 2038 with nothing ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you have kids in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe around thirty-two, after I've switched jobs. I'd want to be settled in the new job first. That's not set in stone, though.

say: I'd say **ten years** is enough to handle this fairly, so no excuses.
I'd compare it to **climate change**: we know it's coming, so plan for it.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** when robots arrive, a good age to have already switched.
The tills are fine for a few **more years** while we get settled.
do: Buy the **flat** with Tomas next year as we planned.
Do the supervisor course first, then a **care course** around thirty.
feel: Pretty **calm**, because ten years is a lot of life.
S4.quote: I'd be thirty-seven when the robots arrive, which is a good age to have already switched.
fieldNote: A decade lets her keep her **flat plan** and stage her career change.
Her worry shifts from herself to **colleagues** who think it's science fiction.
She treats the change like a **planning problem**, not a threat.

steps.text: Buy the flat with Tomas next year as planned
Do the supervisor course, then a care course around thirty
Get retraining written into the next union pay deal

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because nobody would be ready and the shop would just cut us and say sorry. What would help is the company paying for retraining while we still work, plus some kind of income support during the gap. Strong union rules would be the real help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the customers. A lot of old people only talk to anyone when they come to my till. When the tills go, nobody's counting what that costs.

headlineQuote: A lot of old people only talk to anyone when they come to my till.
portrait: Fatima is a **27-year-old** evening cashier at a big superstore, nine years in and a union member.
She has close to a **year's savings** and is buying a flat with Tomas, a bus driver.
She sees her work as **hands-on**, so robots worry her far more than thinking AI.
Across the scenarios she moves from staying put to planning a switch into **care work**.
Her instinct is always to **organise** for colleagues, not only to look after herself.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because nobody would be ready and the shop would simply cut staff.
whatWouldHelp: **Company-paid retraining** while still working, plus income support and strong union rules during the gap.
